title: Mutation Testing Arena — Kill the Mutants
description: Pick one of four small JavaScript functions (leap year, discount, password rules, a digit-sum loop) and breed mutants from its source: arithmetic, relational and logical operator swaps, off-by-one boundary tweaks, return-value flips and forced conditions. Each mutant runs against the test suite in a Blob-built Web Worker with a one-second watchdog. Survivors glow in their petri dishes until you add assertions in the table that kill them, and the mutation score climbs to 100 %.
prompt: Build 'Mutation Testing Arena'. Let me pick a small JS function, such as leap year, a discount calculator or password rules, and show its test suite. Generate mutants: arithmetic, relational and logical operator swaps, boundary tweaks, return-value flips and removed conditions. Run the tests against each mutant right in the page, safely: the functions are local text you control, and each runs in a Web Worker from a Blob with a timeout. Show killed and survived with a mutation score, and let me write extra assertions in a simple table to kill the survivors. Give it a specimen-lab feel: violet ink, acid-green survivors, mutants as petri dishes.

methodology: Hand-derived oracles for the generator: the exact mutant count and survivor count for each built-in suite (leap year 18 mutants with 8 survivors, 56 %; password 9 with 5, 44 %; discount 13 with 6) are asserted, so any change to the tokenizer or the mutation operators shows up at once.

Kill-path tests: adding the textbook boundary cases (1900, 2000; 'Secret12', 'Abcdef1', 'secret123') must take the score to 100 %, and the detail panel must name the assertion that killed a given mutant.

Test-oracle hygiene: assertions are validated against the original function first, so a wrong expectation is flagged with what the original really returns and excluded from the run instead of 'killing' everything.
Sandbox robustness: the digit-sum loop produces two non-terminating mutants; the watchdog must terminate the worker, count them as killed by timeout and leave the page usable for the next run.
Input validation on the assertion form (JSON arguments and expected value) with aria-invalid and a message, plus persistence of user assertions through reload.
risks: Tokenizing regex literals (/[0-9]/) as division operators would produce nonsense mutants; the tokenizer tracks regex context.
A hung mutant blocking the queue: each run waits on a promise that is resolved by either a message or the 1 s watchdog, and a fresh worker is spawned after termination.
Stale results racing a function switch mid-run; runs carry a token and are abandoned when superseded.
Floating-point expectations (200 × 0.9) compared with an epsilon rather than strict equality.
qa.playwright: The awkward part is asynchrony: mutants run one after another in a real Web Worker, so tests wait on a single data-state='done' attribute on the arena instead of sleeping, with an explicit timeout for the run that includes two 1-second hangs. Every petri dish exposes data-id, data-cat and data-status, so assertions such as 'exactly two timeouts' or 'survivors are only Arithmetic and Boundary' are simple locator counts and evaluateAll calls. There is no randomness: mutant IDs follow source order, which is what makes M09 and M15 stable handles. Blob workers count as same-origin, so the site-wide no-external-requests check still holds.
coverage: Baseline run, survivor filter, categories, mutant diff in the source, hint text
Killing all leap-year mutants, the killer named in the detail, persistence
Invalid JSON, wrong expectations flagged and excluded, row deletion, killing the password survivors
Infinite-loop mutants killed by the watchdog; switching functions after a hang

a11y: Functions, filters and mutants are real buttons with aria-pressed, and each petri dish has a full label: ID, category, line, the change, and its fate. Counts and form errors are announced in live regions, inputs have visible labels and aria-invalid, and colour is never the only signal because every dish also says 'survived' or 'killed by …' in text.
